## Introduction
The Paper "Children's understanding of most is dependent on context" by Hurst and Levine explores childrens understanding of the quantifyer "most" in different discrete and continuous contexts. The study had a total of 120 children, 40 4-year-olds, 40 5-year-olds, and 40 6-year-olds. The discrete scenario had children view two sets of obejects, each with different amounts and owned by different characters, and then pick which set owned by which character lost 'most' of their objects (e.g. who broke the most drums?) . The continuous scenario had children view continous areas, with a portion covered by an X, to which children had to pick which area was the 'most' lost (e.g. who had the most sand?) 60 of the children, 20 from each age group, were shown the discrete scenario first, with the other half of the children starting with the continuous scenario first. Researchers evaluated their rate of correct proportional responses. Our focus on the data will be analyzing to determine how performance on the Discrete Block change over time as a function of age. 



## Exploration
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
most_data <- read_csv("Most_tidy.csv")
```

```{r}
most_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = TrialNumber, y = SelectProportion)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  stat_summary(geom = "pointrange", fun.data = "mean_se")
```

```{r}
most_data |> 
ggplot(data=most_data, mapping=aes(y=AgeYears,x=Gender)) + 
  geom_point(alpha=0.5) + stat_summary(geom="pointrange",fun.data = "mean_se", color="purple")

```
